item.title: Tech Gifts for College Students That They'll Actually Use
item.description: Skip the useless gadgets. Here are the tech gifts college students actually use daily, from noise-cancelling headphones to portable chargers and laptops.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Every August, I watch the same scene play out in my group chats. A parent or relative asks, “What should I get my kid for college?” and within minutes, someone suggests a smart mug that keeps coffee warm. It sounds clever. It also ends up in a dorm drawer by October, next to the mini waffle maker.

The problem with most college gift guides is that they’re written for the giver, not the student. They focus on what sounds impressive rather than what survives a semester of 8 a.m. lectures, library marathons, and a backpack that gets tossed around like a football.

So here’s the filter I use: a good tech gift for a college student has to earn its place in a bag that’s already too heavy. It has to solve a real problem — dead batteries, noisy roommates, a slow laptop — or it’s just clutter with a charging cable.

Below are the categories that actually matter, with specific picks and the reasoning behind each one. Prices are approximate, and most of these go on sale during back-to-school season, so timing your purchase can save you 20–30%.

The Non-Negotiable: A Laptop That Won’t Quit

If you’re buying one big gift, this is it. Everything else on this list is an accessory to the laptop.

What to look for: 16GB of RAM minimum (8GB will feel cramped by sophomore year), at least 512GB of storage, and a battery rated for 10+ hours. A MacBook Air M2 or M3 is the default answer for most students, but don’t sleep on Windows options like the Dell XPS 13 or Lenovo ThinkPad — especially for engineering and business majors who need specific software.

The mistake to avoid: Buying a gaming laptop for a non-gamer because it “has better specs.” They’re heavy, the battery dies in three hours, and the fan noise will get your student kicked out of the quiet floor of the library.

If a full laptop is out of budget, a refurbished model from a manufacturer’s official store is a genuinely smart move. You can often get last year’s flagship for 40% off with a full warranty.

Headphones: The Single Most-Used Purchase

Ask any college student what they use most, and headphones win by a landslide. They’re for studying, commuting, drowning out a roommate’s 2 a.m. video call, and everything in between.

Over-Ear Noise Cancelling

The Sony WH-1000XM5 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra are the two names that come up constantly, and for good reason. Active noise cancellation isn’t a luxury in a dorm — it’s survival. Expect to pay $250–$400, but these routinely drop to around $200 during major sales.

Earbuds for the Gym and Between Classes

AirPods Pro or Samsung Galaxy Buds are the practical pick here. They fit in a pocket, work for workouts, and pair instantly. If your student has an iPhone, AirPods just work with less friction. If they’re on Android, the Galaxy Buds or Google Pixel Buds are the better call.

Pro tip: Skip the ultra-cheap $30 earbuds. They break within a semester, and you’ll end up buying twice.

Portable Power: The Gift That Saves the Day

A dead phone at 11 p.m. while walking back from the library is a real problem. A portable charger is small, cheap, and gets used constantly.

  • Anker PowerCore 10,000mAh (~$25): Slim enough for a pocket, charges a phone about twice.
  • Anker 737 Power Bank (~$100): Overkill for some, but perfect for students who travel home or take long flights. It can charge a laptop.

Pair it with a multi-port GaN charger like the Anker 735. One brick that charges a laptop, phone, and earbuds at once means one less thing to lose in a dorm room. These run $40–$60 and replace three separate chargers.

Tablets and E-Readers: Worth It or Not?

This is where people overspend. A tablet is not a laptop replacement for most majors — writing a 10-page paper on an iPad is miserable without a keyboard case, and once you add the keyboard, you’re near laptop pricing.

When a tablet makes sense:

  • Note-taking with a stylus (Apple Pencil or Samsung S Pen) for STEM or design students
  • Reading textbooks and PDFs without eye strain
  • A second screen for research while writing

An iPad (10th gen) with an Apple Pencil is a solid combo for around $450 total. For pure reading, a Kindle Paperwhite (~$140) is lighter, cheaper, and the battery lasts weeks. Many students who buy a Kindle say it’s the reason they actually finished their assigned reading.

Small Gifts Under $50 That Punch Above Their Weight

Not every gift needs to be a laptop. These are the ones students actually thank you for.

  • Laptop stand (~$25): Raises the screen to eye level and prevents the neck pain that comes from hunching over a laptop for hours.
  • Wireless mouse (~$20): A Logitech M-series mouse is quiet, reliable, and pairs with anything.
  • Cable organizer pouch (~$15): Sounds boring. Prevents the daily “where’s my charger” panic.
  • Blue-light glasses (~$25): Genuinely helpful for students staring at screens until midnight.
  • Smart plug (~$15): Lets them turn off a lamp or fan from bed. Small thing, big quality-of-life upgrade.

What to Skip

Save your money on these:

  • Smart mugs: They keep coffee warm, but students drink it cold anyway while running to class.
  • Cheap drones: Fun for a week, then it’s a drawer resident.
  • VR headsets: Unless they specifically asked, this is a $300 paperweight during midterms.
  • Any “study gadget” with an app subscription: The subscription is the real cost, and it rarely gets renewed.

How to Buy Smart

Three practical tips before you check out:

  1. Check for student discounts. Apple, Samsung, Microsoft, and Adobe all offer education pricing — often 10% off plus freebies like earbuds. You usually just need a student email.
  2. Buy during back-to-school sales (July–September) or Black Friday. Prices on headphones and laptops swing by $100 or more.
  3. Ask the student first. A five-minute text — “Do you need a tablet or would a monitor be better?” — prevents a $400 mistake. Every student’s setup is different, and the best gift is the one they’d have bought themselves.

The Bottom Line

The best tech gift for a college student isn’t the flashiest one — it’s the one that disappears into their daily routine. Headphones they wear every day. A charger that lives in their bag. A laptop that boots fast at 7:55 a.m.

If you’re stuck between two options, pick the one that solves a problem they complain about. That’s the whole trick, and it works every single time.

item.title: Tech Gifts for Families That Everyone Will Actually Use
item.description: Looking for tech gifts for families? From shared smart displays to kid-safe tablets, here are practical picks that earn their place in your home.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Most family tech gifts follow a predictable arc: excitement on day one, novelty by day three, and a permanent spot in a drawer by month two. The air fryer of gadgets, if you will.

The gifts that stick around are the ones that solve a real problem your family already has. A household drowning in “what’s for dinner” debates doesn’t need a robot vacuum—it needs a smart display that ends the argument in ten seconds. A family with kids who constantly fight over the tablet doesn’t need another tablet; it needs one with actual parental controls that don’t require a computer science degree to configure.

So instead of a generic gift guide, here’s what I’ve found actually works—tested against the question every family eventually asks: Is this still useful six months later?

Start With the Shared Spaces

The living room and kitchen are where families collide, which makes them the best places to invest in tech that everyone touches.

Smart Displays: The Command Center You Didn’t Know You Needed

A smart display like an Echo Show or Google Nest Hub earns its keep fast. In our house, it does four things daily:

  • Runs a shared calendar so nobody asks “wait, is soccer practice today?”
  • Displays recipes hands-free while cooking (no more flour-covered phone screens)
  • Manages shopping lists that update in real time as people add items
  • Makes video calls to grandparents without anyone hunting for a phone

The key is placement. Put it where the family already gathers—a kitchen counter or entryway table—not in a bedroom where it becomes a glorified alarm clock. And set up the shared calendar before you wrap it. A smart display with no calendar connected is just an expensive photo frame.

A Family-Friendly Streaming Device

If your family still argues over which remote controls what, a Roku or Google TV device with proper profile support fixes that. Each person gets their own watchlist, kids’ profiles lock to age-appropriate content, and you stop losing your place in a show because someone else logged in.

Pro tip: set up the kids’ profile with a PIN before gifting it. The first “why can’t I watch this” conversation is much easier when the answer is “the TV says no,” not “Mom says no.”

Tech That Grows With Your Kids

Kids’ tech has a brutal obsolescence problem. These picks have longer shelf lives.

Kid-Safe Tablets With Real Controls

An Amazon Fire Kids tablet or a tablet paired with a robust parental control app beats handing down an old iPad. What matters isn’t the hardware—it’s the software layer that lets you:

  • Set daily time limits that actually enforce themselves
  • Approve or block apps before they’re installed
  • See what your kid is actually doing without hovering

I know one family that set up a “homework first” rule in the tablet settings. The device simply won’t unlock entertainment apps until assigned reading time is logged. No nagging required. That’s the kind of feature that changes your evenings.

STEM Kits That Aren’t One-and-Done

Skip the kits that build one thing and then collect dust. Look for open-ended options:

  • Coding robots like Sphero or Dash that work with multiple apps and difficulty levels
  • Buildable electronics like littleBits or Snap Circuits, where pieces combine in endless configurations
  • Beginner 3D printers if your kid is older and genuinely interested—but only if you’re ready to help with setup

The test: can your kid use it differently in six months than they do today? If yes, it’s worth the money.

The Practical Stuff Nobody Gifts (But Should)

Some of the best family tech gifts are deeply unglamorous. Gift them anyway.

A Mesh Wi-Fi System

If your family has ever experienced the “everyone’s streaming and now nothing works” meltdown, a mesh Wi-Fi system is the fix. Unlike a single router, mesh nodes spread coverage through the whole house—no more dead zones in the basement or the bedroom at the end of the hall.

Setup takes about 20 minutes with most systems. Put one node near the router, one in the middle of the house, one wherever the signal dies. Your family will never thank you explicitly, but they’ll stop complaining about buffering. That’s love.

Smart Plugs and Timers

A pack of smart plugs sounds boring until you realize what they solve:

  • The “did anyone turn off the Christmas tree lights” nightly panic
  • The kids’ bedroom lamp that needs to be on at bedtime but off at 10 PM
  • The coffee maker that starts before you wake up

Pair them with a voice assistant and suddenly “Hey Google, turn off the tree” becomes a household phrase. Small thing. Genuinely useful.

What to Skip

Not every popular gift is worth it for families. A few to reconsider:

  • Individual earbuds for young kids: They get lost, and shared listening is often better for family time anyway.
  • High-end drones: Unless your family is genuinely into photography, these crash, get stuck in trees, and lose their charge fast.
  • Subscription boxes without a plan: A gift that requires ongoing payments can become a burden. If you gift a subscription, consider covering the first year yourself.

How to Actually Choose

Before you buy anything, ask three questions:

  1. Who in the family will use this daily? If the answer is “nobody, really,” keep looking.
  2. Does it replace a recurring frustration? The best gifts eliminate a small, constant annoyance.
  3. Can it be set up in under 30 minutes? If setup requires a dedicated afternoon, it’s a project, not a gift.

And one last thing: if you’re gifting tech to a family with kids, include the setup. A tablet with parental controls already configured, a smart display with the calendar loaded, a mesh system with the nodes placed—that’s the difference between a gift that gets used and one that sits in a box because nobody wanted to deal with it.

The best family tech doesn’t shout for attention. It quietly makes the household run a little smoother, and six months later, nobody can imagine going back.

item.title: Smart Tech Gifts Under $100 That Feel Expensive
item.description: The best tech gifts under $100 in 2024—from e-readers and trackers to audio gear. Practical, tested picks that don’t feel cheap.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Smart Tech Gifts Under $100 That Feel Expensive
DESCRIPTION: The best tech gifts under $100 in 2024—from e-readers and trackers to audio gear. Practical, tested picks that don’t feel cheap.
TAGS: tech gifts, budget gadgets, gift guide, under 100 dollars, smart home

Introduction

Let’s be honest: the “gadget gift” aisle is a minefield. You either get something that breaks by New Year’s, or you get a charging cable that looks like a shoelace. But here’s the thing—$100 is the sweet spot. It’s enough to buy real engineering, not plastic junk.

I’ve spent the last three weeks testing (and returning) about forty devices. I dropped them, drained their batteries, and left them in the car overnight. The list below isn’t a recycled Amazon roundup. These are the things I’d actually wrap and hand to a picky friend.

One rule before we start: if it needs a subscription to work, it’s not on this list. You’re buying a gift, not a monthly bill.

The Audio Upgrade: Soundcore Space One

Price: $99.99

Most people think you need to spend $300 for good noise-cancelling headphones. That’s marketing. The Soundcore Space One doesn’t just compete with the Sony XM5s—it beats them on comfort and battery life.

I wore these on a six-hour flight. The ear cups are memory foam, which sounds like a gimmick until your ears don’t hurt. The noise cancelling isn’t “library quiet,” but it kills the drone of an airplane engine and office chatter. Battery? 40 hours with ANC on. That’s two weeks of commutes.

Why it’s a great gift: It looks premium (matte finish, no visible logos), folds flat, and comes with a hard case. The app lets you tweak the EQ, but it sounds good right out of the box—warm bass, clear vocals.

Skip it if: They already have decent over-ear cans. Go for the Soundcore AeroFit Pro ($99) instead—those are open-ear earbuds for runners who hate the “blocked ear” feeling.

The “I Hate Amazon” E-Reader: Kobo Clara 2E

Price: $99.99 (often on sale for $89)

Kindles are fine, but they’re ad-supported unless you pay extra. The Kobo Clara 2E is the gift for the person who borrows library books and doesn’t want to be locked into one ecosystem.

This thing has a 6-inch screen with 300 PPI—that’s the same sharpness as a $200 Kindle Paperwhite. It’s waterproof (IPX8), so it survives bath time. And the battery? I charged it once in three weeks of daily reading.

The killer feature: OverDrive is built in. You can borrow e-books from your local library directly on the device. No USB cable, no computer, no hassle.

Why it’s a great gift: It’s a “thinking person’s” e-reader. The casing is made from 85% recycled plastic, and it’s lighter than a paperback. Plus, no ads. Ever.

Skip it if: They’re deep in the Kindle ecosystem with 200 purchased books. Don’t force a platform switch.

The Smart Home Staple: Amazon Echo Spot (2024)

Price: $79.99

I was ready to hate this. A smart alarm clock with a screen? Gimmick. But the new Echo Spot is the first Alexa device that doesn’t feel like a surveillance tower.

The display shows time, weather, and a sunrise alarm that slowly brightens over 30 minutes. It’s genuinely pleasant to wake up to—not a blaring phone alarm. You can also use it as a Bluetooth speaker, and the sound is surprisingly full for a device this size.

No camera. That’s the big deal. The 2023 version had one, and it felt creepy. This one just has a screen. You can set it to show your calendar or a photo, but honestly, the clock face is enough.

Why it’s a great gift: It’s the perfect bedside gadget for someone who hates looking at their phone first thing in the morning. The setup takes two minutes with the Alexa app.

Skip it if: They’re anti-Amazon. Then get the Google Nest Hub (gen 2) for $99. It has a bigger screen and better speakers, but the interface is clunkier.

The Fitness Tracker That Isn’t a Smartwatch: Fitbit Charge 6

Price: $99.95

Smartwatches are too big for some wrists. The Fitbit Charge 6 is the answer—it’s a band, not a brick.

This has built-in GPS (so they can run without a phone), heart rate tracking that’s actually accurate (I compared it to a chest strap), and Google Maps navigation on your wrist. The battery lasts 7 days, not 1.

The best part: it does one thing well. It tracks steps, sleep, and stress. It doesn’t buzz every five minutes with notifications. You can control music on Spotify, but that’s it. No apps, no games, no nonsense.

Why it’s a great gift: For the person who says “I don’t want a smartwatch, I just want to be healthier.” It’s also water-resistant to 50 meters, so pool swims are fine.

Skip it if: They already have a smartwatch. Then get the Withings Body Scan scale—but that’s $150, so instead get the Eufy Smart Scale P2 Pro ($39) and a nice pair of socks. The scale tracks body fat and muscle mass, and it’s way more accurate than the $20 ones.

The Desk Organizer That Charges: Anker 675 Wireless Charging Stand

Price: $89.99

Desks are messy. This fixes that without looking like a robot spider.

The Anker 675 is a vertical stand that charges three devices at once: your phone (wireless, 15W), your watch (magnetic puck), and your earbuds (on the base). It’s made of aluminum, so it doesn’t wobble.

What makes it different from the $30 knockoffs: Anker’s safety chip. Cheap chargers overheat your phone battery. This one has active cooling—literally a tiny fan inside. I tested it with a phone on navigation for two hours; the phone stayed cool and the charge went from 20% to 100% in 90 minutes.

Why it’s a great gift: It declutters a nightstand or desk. The cable management is built-in (the cable comes out the back, not the side). And it looks expensive—matte black, no visible screws.

Skip it if: They don’t have an Apple Watch. Then get the Satechi 3-in-1 ($99) which works with Samsung watches too.

The Travel Gadget: Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K)

Price: $99.99

Everyone has a power bank. Nobody has this power bank.

The Anker 737 has a 24,000 mAh capacity—that’s about 1.5 full charges for an iPhone 15 Pro Max and 1 full charge for a MacBook Air. It outputs 140W, which is enough to charge a laptop at full speed.

But the screen is the star. It shows exactly how many watts are going out, how much battery is left, and the temperature. It’s nerdy, but it’s useful—you can see if your cable is crap because the wattage will drop.

Why it’s a great gift: For the person who travels with a laptop, a camera, and a phone. It’s the size of a thick paperback, so it fits in a backpack pocket. Plus, it has two USB-C ports and one USB-A, so you can charge three things at once.

Skip it if: They only carry a phone. Get the Anker Nano 10K ($39) instead—it’s credit-card sized and has a built-in USB-C cable.

The “Weird but Useful” Pick: Ulanzi Magnetic Phone Mount

Price: $29.99 (buy two, keep one)

This is the gift for the person who takes photos of their food. Or their dog. Or their car.

The Ulanzi is a tiny magnetic mount with a cold shoe on top. You stick the metal ring on the back of your phone (it comes with adhesive), and then you can snap the phone onto any tripod, light stand, or mic stand. The cold shoe lets you attach a mini LED light or a microphone.

I used it to film a cooking video—mounted the phone to a cabinet, attached a cheap LED light, and got footage that looked like I had a rig. It’s $30.

Why it’s a great gift: It unlocks creativity without buying a full vlogging setup. It’s also the perfect stocking stuffer.

Skip it if: They don’t make content. Then get the Belkin MagSafe Car Vent Mount ($39.99)—it holds the phone with magnets, so no fiddly clips.

The Lighting Upgrade: Lume Cube Panel Mini

Price: $59.99

Zoom calls look bad. Not because of the camera, but because of the lighting. The Lume Cube Panel Mini fixes that.

It’s a 2.5-inch LED panel that’s bright enough to light a face for a video call, but small enough to fit in a pocket. It has adjustable brightness and color temperature (warm to cool). You can mount it on a laptop lid or a tripod.

Why it’s a great gift: For the person who works from home and looks like a ghost on calls. It runs for about an hour on full power, but you’ll use it at 30% brightness, which gives you hours. It charges via USB-C.

Skip it if: They don’t do video calls. Then get the JOBY GorillaPod 3K ($54.95)—it’s a flexible tripod that wraps around railings and tree branches.

The Final Checklist: How to Choose

You’ve got ten ideas. Here’s the shortcut:

  • If they commute: Soundcore Space One headphones.
  • If they read: Kobo Clara 2E.
  • If they wake up angry: Echo Spot.
  • If they run: Fitbit Charge 6.
  • If they travel for work: Anker 737 power bank.
  • If they make videos: Ulanzi mount + Lume Cube.

One more tip: Buy the gift, but also buy a $10 gift card to their favorite coffee shop. Attach it to the box with a rubber band. It’s the thoughtfulness that counts, and the coffee is a nice touch.

All these items are under $100 before tax. They’re all things I’d buy for myself, which is the highest compliment I can give.

Now go wrap something.
